dati_metodo: US VC deals 1976-2017 (Refinitiv VentureXpert) matched to all US patents; panel regressions of deal volume and patent quality on NBER recession months; plus COVID-19 early look with PitchBook and CB Insights deal counts (March-April 2020)

righe.estrazione: Using monthly Refinitiv data on US VC deals, the paper shows that early-stage investment falls sharply in NBER recessions, far more than later-stage investment, for dollar volume, number of deals and deal size. Early-stage dollars fall by 39% and deal counts by 33%, while later-stage activity shows no measurable relationship with recessions. The COVID-19 episode shows the same pattern (early-stage deals down about 38%).
righe.citazione: Investments in early-stage transactions fall off sharply in recessions, far more so than later-stage ones.
righe.posizione: 4.1 The impact of earlier recessions on venture investment
righe.frase_paper: Howell et al. (2020) find that early-stage VC investment falls sharply in NBER recessions between 1976 and 2017, far more than later-stage investment, which shows no measurable relationship with recessions.
righe.frase_slide: Early-stage VC drops sharply in recessions, later-stage barely moves (Howell et al., 2020)
righe.numero_chiave: In recessions early-stage VC dollars fall by 39% and the number of early-stage deals by 33% (Table 1, Panel A, columns 1 and 4)
righe.limiti_vs_noi: Recessions (NBER peak to trough) over 1976-2017, deal-level volume not startup outcomes; our sample is 2012-2019 with no recession and hype is a sector share of VC dollars, not a downturn indicator.
righe.note: 'Falls most' is read as relative to later-stage; the txt states the difference is statistically significant. Association, not causal.

righe.estrazione: The paper does not study follow-on funding of individual startups. Its capital-supply evidence is about patent quality: startups that raised their latest round just before a recession (more runway) are less affected, which the authors say supports a capital-supply story. Capital supply is also one of several mechanisms said to be at play; the follow-on funding logic is attributed to Nanda and Rhodes-Kropf (2017) and Townsend (2015), not shown here.
righe.citazione: In sum, this exercise supports the capital supply story.
righe.limiti_vs_noi: Outcome is patent quality of VC-backed firms, not probability of a second round or exit.
righe.note: Closest supportable claim: timing of the last round matters for patent quality in recessions, consistent with capital supply (Table 11). Follow-on funding itself is only theorised via others' work.

righe.estrazione: The paper shows that VC deal activity is strongly pro-cyclical: it falls in recessions, especially early-stage. On whether the cause is supply, it is more cautious: all forces (investment opportunities, entrepreneurs' human capital, supply frictions) are likely at play, and the early-stage concentration and the fundraising-timing test are said to suggest or support a capital-supply friction. In the COVID-19 episode the authors argue supply was not constrained.
righe.citazione: All of these forces are likely at play, to a greater or lesser extent, in recessions.
righe.frase_paper: Howell et al. (2020) show that VC deal activity falls in recessions, especially at the early stage, and argue that frictions in the supply of capital are a likely, though not the only, mechanism.
righe.frase_slide: VC activity falls in recessions; supply frictions are a likely, not sole, channel (Howell et al., 2020)
righe.numero_chiave: Early-stage VC deals down about 38% in the two months from 4 March 2020 vs the previous four months
righe.limiti_vs_noi: Recession and COVID-19 shocks, not within-sector hype variation in a boom period; patent-quality tests, no startup exit outcomes.
righe.note: Compound tesi: 'follows the economy down' is shown; 'supply-side variation' is only suggestive and one of several mechanisms, which decided the esito.
